title: Choose between a platter service and a live counter
focus: A chilled platter and a chef-led sushi counter create different experiences and require different facilities. Discuss the balance of rolls, nigiri, cooked choices and vegetarian alternatives alongside the venue and service duration. Chilled storage and replenishment need to be assessed for the actual setting, particularly outdoors or on a yacht. Share seafood allergies and other ingredient requirements early. The menu should be chosen with the preparation and holding arrangements in mind, rather than treating appearance as the only consideration.

sections.title: Choose between platters and a sushi counter
paragraphs: Platters suit a defined serving time and a venue with appropriate chilled storage. A live counter creates a different experience, with a chef preparing or finishing agreed items during service. Tell us whether sushi is a light reception selection, one part of a buffet or the main food for the gathering.

Discuss the balance of fish, cooked items and vegetarian choices before choosing quantities. Share allergies and ingredient restrictions, including seafood, soy and sesame where relevant. The team must assess preparation arrangements and cross-contact risks; a different menu may be more appropriate for some guests.

Confirm when the food will be prepared, delivered and served, and who manages refrigeration and replenishment at the venue. Yacht catering needs an additional check of loading times, galley facilities and the charter schedule. Your proposal should make the menu, staffing, equipment and agreed service window clear.

sections.title: Give every guest a considered option
paragraphs: Collect dietary requirements before the final menu is agreed. Record how many guests each requirement applies to and distinguish preferences from allergies or other essential restrictions. A clear list helps the culinary team assess suitable dishes and the preparation arrangements they would need.

A vegetarian or vegan choice should feel like a complete part of the menu. Consider its portion, accompaniments and presentation alongside the other dishes, rather than removing an ingredient and assuming the result will be satisfying. Sauces, garnishes, breads and desserts also need attention.

Allergy requests require a specific discussion of ingredients and kitchen conditions. Labels and separate serving utensils can support a plan, but they do not by themselves guarantee the absence of cross-contact. Share the details early so the team can assess the request honestly and confirm what can be accommodated before you book.

sections.title: List the equipment before calling the plan complete
paragraphs: Food, kitchen equipment and table items are separate parts of a catering brief. Confirm what the venue supplies and what the catering team needs to bring. Depending on the format, that may include preparation equipment, holding equipment, serving utensils, crockery, glassware or linen.

A photograph of a styled event does not establish what is included in your own package. If you want the same type of table setup or service display, ask for those items to be identified in the proposal. This is particularly useful when the property has limited kitchen facilities or the event uses more than one dining area.

Also agree how equipment will arrive, be set up and be collected. Access restrictions and collection times can affect the plan. A clear equipment list helps the team prepare properly and gives you a practical way to check that the venue is ready before guests arrive.
